title: Does Aid Matter? Measuring the Effect of Student Aid on College Attendance and Completion
research_question: Does eligibility for grant-based student financial aid increase the probability that young people attend college and the amount of schooling they ultimately complete? How large is the response of college enrollment and completed years of schooling to a given dollar increase in available grant aid?
data_description: The analysis uses the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY), specifically the cross-section and poverty subsamples, with respondents followed from 1979 onward and weighted using 1988 sample weights. The unit of observation is an individual youth. Key variables include full-time college attendance since high-school senior year, highest grade completed measured at ages 23 and 28, age-adjusted AFQT percentile (test administered in 1980), senior-year family income (in $2,000 dollars), parental education and survival status, household composition, family size, race, Hispanic origin, gender, age, and state of residence. The estimation sample comprises 3,986 individuals who were high-school seniors between 1979 and 1983, split into pre-policy cohorts (seniors in 1979–1981) and post-policy cohorts (seniors in 1982–1983), and further distinguished by whether the respondent's father was deceased before the youth turned 18.
institutional_context: From 1965 through 1982, the Social Security Administration paid monthly cash benefits to 18- to 22-year-old children of deceased, disabled, or retired Social Security beneficiaries, conditional on full-time college enrollment. At its 1977 peak, roughly 700,000 students received benefits, and in 1980 the average annual payment to a child of a deceased parent was about $6,700 (in $2,000 dollars)—enough to cover tuition and fees at public four-year universities and far exceeding the average Pell Grant. Benefits were paid as lump-sum monthly checks with minimal application requirements and no link to actual schooling costs. In 1981, Congress voted to end the program: students not enrolled by May 1982 became ineligible, and existing recipients faced a sharp phaseout, cutting program spending by roughly $3 billion by 1984–1985. This abrupt termination represents one of the largest discrete changes in U.S. grant aid for college students.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The main finding is that student aid substantially increases college attendance. Students who received aid due to the Social Security Student Benefit Program were significantly more likely to attend college compared to those who lost eligibility.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: ~3.6 percentage point increase in college attendance per $1,000 of aid
key_robustness: varying time windows around the policy change
